question_text: In the context of liver function tests, what does a prolonged prothrombin time (PT) indicate?
option_c: Impaired synthetic function of the liver
explanation:
Explanation:

A prolonged prothrombin time (PT) suggests that the liver is not adequately producing clotting factors, which are essential for blood coagulation.

Because these clotting factors are synthesized in the liver, a prolonged PT is an indicator of impaired liver synthetic function.

  • Prothrombin Time (PT): Prolonged PT reflects impaired liver synthetic function. The liver produces clotting factors (II, VII, IX, X) dependent on vitamin K, and dysfunction results in reduced production.
  • Vitamin K's Role: While reduced vitamin K intake can contribute to prolonged PT, the liver must also be functioning properly to utilize vitamin K effectively.
  • Liver Function Tests (LFTs): Other tests such as albumin, bilirubin, ALT, AST, and ALP also provide insights into various aspects of liver function like synthetic ability, excretion, and injury.

Explanation for the other options:

  • Prolonged PT does not indicate increased liver function. It suggests reduced production of clotting factors due to impaired synthetic activity.
  • While vitamin K deficiency can prolong PT, liver dysfunction is more commonly the underlying cause in the context of liver disease.
  • Platelets are unrelated to PT. They influence primary hemostasis, while PT reflects the synthesis of clotting factors involved in secondary hemostasis.

Level:

Moderate

question_text: Substitution of base can result in:
explanation:
Single-base changes (point mutations) may be transitions or transversions. In the former, a given pyrimidine is changed to the other pyrimidine or a given purine is changed to the other purine. Transversions are changes from a purine to either of the two pyrimidines or the change of a pyrimidine into either of the two purines.

When the nucleotide sequence of a protein-coding gene containing the mutation is transcribed into an mRNA molecule, then the RNA molecule will of course possess the base change at the corresponding location.

Single-base changes in the mRNA may have one of several effects when translated into protein:

  1. There may be no detectable effect because of the degeneracy of the code; such mutations are often referred to as silent This would be most likely if the changed base in the mRNA molecule were to be at the third nucleotide of a codon. Because of wobble, the translation of a codon is least sensitive to a change at the third position. A missense effect will occur when a different amino acid is incorporated at the corresponding site in the protein molecule. This mistaken amino acid-or missense, depending on its location in the specific protein-might be acceptable, partially acceptable, or unacceptable to the function of that protein molecule.
  2. A nonsense codon may appear that would then result in the premature termination of translation and the production of only a fragment of the intended protein molecule. The probability is high that a prematurely terminated protein molecule or peptide fragment will not function in its normal role.

So Substitution of base results in Silent mutation (Option A), Missense mutation (Option B), & Nonsense mutation (Option C). the correct answer is Option D.

Reference: Harper's illustrated biochemistry 32nd edition CH 37 PN 397

question_text: Which of the following is true regarding messenger RNA?
option_a: 5' terminal end has poly A tail
option_b: 3' terminal end is capped by 7 methyl guanosine triphosphate
option_d: Pre mRNA is shorter than mature mRNA molecule
explanation:
Option A: 5’ terminal end is capped by 7 methyl guanosine triphosphate

Option B: 3’ terminal end has poly A tail.

Option C: Messenger RNA is the most heterogeneous in abundance, size, and stability. 

Option D: In mammalian cell nuclei, the immediate products of gene transcription (primary transcripts or pre mRNA) are very heterogeneous and can be greater than 10- to 50-fold longer than mature mRNA molecules. Such pre-mRNA molecules are processed to generate mRNA molecules, which then enter the cytoplasm to serve as templates for protein synthesis.

Messenger RNA 

Messenger RNA is the most heterogeneous in abundance, size, and stability. A specific transcriptional and posttranscriptional mechanisms contribute to this large dynamic range in mRNA content.

All members of this RNA class function as messengers conveying the information in a gene to the protein-synthesizing machinery, where each mRNA serves as a template on which a specific sequence of amino acids is polymerized to form a specific protein molecule, the ultimate gene product.

Both the mRNA “cap” and “poly(A) tail” are added posttranscriptionally by nontemplate-directed enzymes to mRNA precursor molecules (pre-mRNA).

mRNA represents 2 to 5% of total eukaryotic cellular RNA. 

In mammalian cells, including cells of humans, the mRNA molecules present in the cytoplasm are not the RNA products immediately synthesized from the DNA template but must be formed by processing from the precursor, or pre-mRNA before entering the cytoplasm. Thus, in mammalian cell nuclei, the immediate products of gene transcription (primary transcripts) are very heterogeneous and can be greater than 10- to 50-fold longer than mature mRNA molecules. Such pre-mRNA molecules are processed to generate mRNA molecules, which then enter the cytoplasm to serve as templates for protein synthesis.

Reference: Harper's illustrated biochemistry 32nd edition CH 34 PN 344

question_text: Which of the following RNA is specifically used to decrease specific protein levels?
explanation:
Option A: siRNAs

The small non coding RNAs (ncRNAs) termed miRNAs (Micro-RNAs) and siRNAs (Silencing RNAs) typically inhibit gene expression at the level of specific protein production by targeting mRNAs through one of several distinct mechanisms. siRNAs are frequently used to decrease or “knockdown” specific protein levels (via siRNA homology–directed mRNA degradation) in experimental contexts in the laboratory.

Option B: circRNAs:

There are two classes of larger noncoding RNAs: the circular RNAs (circRNAs) and the long noncoding RNAs, or lncRNAs.

Many circRNAs have recently been discovered and characterized. circRNAs appear to be produced by RNA splicing-type reactions from a wide range of precursor RNAs, both mRNA precursors and nonprotein lncRNA precursors. Though not an abundant class of RNA molecules in most cells, circRNAs have been detected in all eukaryotes tested, particularly in metazoans. While the functions of circRNAs are still being elucidated they seem to be particularly abundant in cells of the nervous system. Similar to lncRNAs, these molecules likely play important roles in cellular biology by regulating gene expression at multiple levels.

Option C: Small Nuclear RNAs (snRNAs), a subset of the small nuclear RNAs are significantly involved in rRNA and mRNA processing and gene regulation.

Option D: Ribosomal RNA

A ribosome is a cytoplasmic nucleoprotein structure that acts as the machinery for the synthesis of proteins from the mRNA templates. On the ribosomes, the mRNA and tRNA molecules interact to translate the information transcribed from the gene during mRNA synthesis into a specific protein.

Reference: Harper's illustrated biochemistry 32nd edition CH 34 PN 347

question_text: Cholera toxin keeps the G αs subunit of G protein in:
explanation:
• The Heterotrimeric G-proteins composed of α, β, and γ subunits.
  • Since the α subunit in Gs differs from that in Gi, the proteins, which are distinct gene products, are designated αs and αi. The α subunits bind guanine nucleotides. The β and γ subunits are likely always associated (βγ) and appear to function predominantly as a heterodimer.
  • The αs subunit has intrinsic GTPase activity. The active form, αs - GTP, is inactivated on hydrolysis of the GTP to GDP; the trimeric Gs complex (αβγ) is then reformed and is ready for another cycle of activation.

question_text: Which biomarker is used to evaluate myocardial injury in the context of chronic heart failure?
explanation:
Explanation:

Cardiac-specific Troponin I:

  • Troponin I is a structural protein released from damaged cardiomyocytes.
  • It provides high specificity and sensitivity for detecting myocardial injury, including ongoing injury in chronic heart failure.
  • Chronic elevation in heart failure suggests progressive myocardial stress or cell death, often associated with poor prognosis.
  • Unlike NT-proBNP, troponins directly reflect cardiomyocyte damage rather than hemodynamic stress.

NT-proBNP:

  • Released in response to increased ventricular wall stress and volume overload.
  • It is widely used for diagnosing and monitoring heart failure, but it is influenced by non-specific factors like renal dysfunction or age.
  • Elevated levels in heart failure do not directly indicate myocardial cell injury.

Adrenomedullin:

  • Plays a role in vascular tone regulation and fluid homeostasis.
  • Elevated in heart failure but lacks specificity for heart muscle injury.
  • Research indicates its potential as a prognostic marker for heart failure severity rather than direct myocardial damage.

Copeptin:

  • A surrogate marker for arginine vasopressin (AVP), reflecting neurohormonal activation in heart failure.
  • Associated with cardiovascular stress and poor outcomes but does not indicate specific myocardial damage.

Key Takeaways:

Troponin I is the most specific biomarker for assessing myocardial injury in chronic heart failure, indicating ongoing cardiomyocyte damage.

NT-proBNP provides insights into heart failure severity and ventricular wall stress, not myocardial damage.

Biomarkers like adrenomedullin and copeptin have emerging roles in prognosis but lack specificity for detecting cardiomyocyte injury.

Moderate

question_text: Proteins can be precipitated by altering their solubility through various physical and chemical methods. These techniques are widely used in laboratory purification protocols. Which of the following is a valid method for precipitation of proteins?
option_c: Precipitation of protein by UV rays
explanation:
Explanation :

Alcohols such as ethanol and isopropanol reduce the dielectric constant of the solution and remove hydration shells around proteins, leading to protein precipitation. This method is commonly used in biochemical laboratories and clinical tests (eg. C-reactive protein precipitation).

  • Organic solvents reduce available water, leading to protein precipitation; alcohol acts as a strong protein precipitating agent and has disinfectant properties.(Option A)
  • Lyophilizationis freeze-drying, removing water from frozen products under vacuum. (Option B)
  • Denaturation: UV rays and heat cause protein denaturation, a mild precipitation reaction; heat coagulation is irreversible. (Options C & D)

Key takeaways: The addition of organic solvents like alcohol reduces water availability and dielectric constant, causing protein precipitation and explaining alcohol's disinfectant effect.

  • Precipitation Methods:
  • Stability Factors: Protein stability relies on charge and hydration; polar groups attract water, and neutralizing charges or removing hydration causes precipitation.
    1. Salting Out: Adding neutral salts (e.g., ammonium sulfate) removes hydration shells, precipitating proteins; higher molecular weight proteins require less salt.
    2. Isoelectric Precipitation: Proteins are least soluble at their isoelectric pH (e.g., casein at pH 4.6).
    3. Precipitation by Organic Solvents: Organic solvents decrease water availability and dielectric constant, leading to precipitation.
    4. Precipitation by Heavy Metal Ions: Heavy metals can complex with proteins, causing precipitation; toxic metals (e.g., copper, mercury) can harm normal gastrointestinal proteins.
    5. Precipitation by Alkaloidal Reagents: Agents like phosphotungstic acid lower pH, causing positively charged proteins to precipitate with negatively charged ions.

question_text: Which type of mutation leads to the restoration of the wild-type phenotype when the mutant gene is suppressed?
explanation:
Explanation:

This concept involves a suppressor mutation, in which a second mutation occurs often in a tRNA gene, that compensates for the defect caused by the primary mutation.

The altered tRNA can recognize the mutant codon and insert the correct amino acid, thereby restoring the wild-type phenotype even though the original mutation remains in the coding gene.

This mechanism effectively suppresses the functional effect of the initial mutation without reversing it.

Suppressor Mutation

A suppressor mutation is a secondary mutation that mitigates or counteracts the effect of a primary mutation, thereby restoring partial or complete gene or protein function.

It does not eliminate the original mutation but compensates for its phenotypic consequences.

Key Features

Types of Suppressor Mutations:

  • Intragenic suppressor: Occurs within the same gene as the primary mutation, often restoring function by altering protein structure or the reading frame.
  • Extragenic suppressor: Occurs in a different gene (commonly a tRNA gene) and restores normal function by modifying translation or gene expression.

Suppressor tRNA

A mutated tRNA that can read abnormal or altered codons caused by missense, nonsense, or frameshift mutations, thereby restoring protein synthesis.

Mechanisms include:

  • Missense suppression: Inserts a compensatory amino acid at the mutated codon.
  • Nonsense suppression: Reads a stop codon as a sense codon, allowing translation to continue.
  • Frameshift suppression: Restores the correct reading frame during translation.

Limitations

Suppressor tRNAs may not distinguish between normal and mutant codons, potentially leading to:

  • Misreading of normal stop codons → formation of abnormally long proteins.
  • Unintended shifts in reading frame → disrupted protein synthesis.

These off-target effects can impair cellular function or viability.

Applications

Laboratory Use:

Engineered suppressor tRNAs, combined with modified aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases, are valuable molecular tools for:

  • Incorporating unnatural amino acids into proteins.
  • Studying protein structure, function, and interactions both in vivo and in vitro.

Explanation of other options:

Frameshift of the Mutated Gene (Option A): A frameshift mutation occurs when nucleotides are inserted or deleted in numbers not divisible by three, leading to a shift in the mRNA reading frame. This change alters the downstream codon sequence, often producing a truncated or nonfunctional protein due to premature stop codons.

Addition of Another Normal Gene (Option B): Introducing a normal copy of a gene into the genome can compensate for the effects of a mutant gene. This concept underlies gene therapy, where the added gene restores normal function. However, this is not considered a mutation, but rather a therapeutic intervention.

Deletion of the Mutated Gene (Option C): Removing the mutated gene eliminates its harmful product but does not automatically restore the wild-type phenotype. Functional recovery would only occur if another mechanism or gene compensates for the loss of the deleted gene.

explanation:
Option A: Integral proteins Interact extensively with the phospholipids. Peripheral proteins do not interact directly with the hydrophobic cores of the phospholipids in the bilayer. They are bound to the hydrophilic regions of specific integral proteins and head groups of phospholipids.

Option B: Integral proteins requires use of detergents for their solubilization. Peripheral proteins do not do not require use of detergents for their release. They can be released from them by treatment with salt solutions of high ionic strength.

Option D: Examples of integral proteins are: transporter molecules, ion channels, various receptors, and G proteins, Glycophorin A.

Examples of peripheral proteins are: Ankyrin, Spectrin So Glycophorin A is an example of integral protein, not peripheral proteins.

Membrane proteins are divided into two types:

Integral proteins and Peripheral proteins

  • Integral proteins interact extensively with the phospholipids and require the use of detergents for their solubilization. Also, they generally span the bilayer as a bundle of α-helical transmembrane segments. Integral proteins are usually globular and are themselves amphipathic. They consist of two hydrophilic ends separated by an intervening hydrophobic region that traverses the hydrophobic core of the bilayer. As the structures of integral membrane proteins were being elucidated, it became apparent that certain ones (e.g., transporter molecules, ion channels, various receptors, and G proteins) span the bilayer many times, whereas other simple membrane proteins (e.g., glycophorin A) span the membrane only once. Integral proteins are asymmetrically distributed across the membrane bilayer. This asymmetric orientation is conferred at the time of their insertion in the lipid bilayer during biosynthesis in the ER
  • Peripheral proteins do not interact directly with the hydrophobic cores of the phospholipids in the bilayer and thus do not require use of detergents for their release. They are bound to the hydrophilic regions of specific integral proteins and head groups of phospholipids and can be released from them by treatment with salt solutions of high ionic strength. For example, ankyrin, a peripheral protein, is bound to the inner aspect of the integral protein “band 3” of the erythrocyte membrane. Spectrin, a cytoskeletal structure within the erythrocyte, is in turn bound to ankyrin and thereby plays an important role in maintenance of the biconcave shape of the erythrocyte.

question_text: What is the origin and type of cell responsible for testosterone production?
explanation:
Explanation:

Testosterone is synthesized primarily in the Leydig cells of the testes.

These cells convert cholesterol into testosterone through enzymatic steps involving 17α-hydroxylase, 17,20-lyase, and 3β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase.

  • Luteinizing hormone (LH) from the anterior pituitary stimulates Leydig cells to initiate this process. Cholesterol may be derived from internal synthesis or uptake from circulating LDL/HDL.

Functions of Leydig Cells

  • Leydig cells are responsible for the secretion of testosterone.
  • Cholesterol is the key precursor in testosterone synthesis. Leydig cells obtain cholesterol either by internal synthesis or by uptake from circulating LDL and HDL through their receptors.
  • They also convert dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA) into testosterone.
  • The testosterone produced diffuses into the seminiferous tubules (adluminal compartment) where it supports spermatogenesis.

Functions of Sertoli Cells

  • Sertoli cells are the only cells that form the blood-testis barrier, providing a protected environment for germ cell development.
  • They supply nutritional and structural support to developing sperm.
  • Sertoli cells have receptors for FSH and androgens, thereby indirectly enhancing spermatogenesis.
  • They produce androgen-binding protein (ABP) to concentrate testosterone within the seminiferous tubules.
  • They express aromatase, which converts testosterone to estrogen.
  • During fetal development, they secrete Anti-Müllerian Hormone (AMH/MIS), which causes regression of Müllerian ducts.
  • Sertoli cells also secrete Inhibin B, which exerts negative feedback on the anterior pituitary to reduce FSH secretion.
  • Additionally, they synthesize extracellular matrix proteins essential for testicular structure.

Cholesterol and Sertoli cells (Option A): Sertoli cells are not responsible for testosterone production. Instead, they support spermatogenesis, form the blood–testis barrier, secrete inhibin B, androgen-binding protein, and express aromatase for estrogen synthesis.

Dihydrotestosterone and Leydig cells (Option B): Dihydrotestosterone (DHT) is not the primary product of Leydig cells. It is formed peripherally from testosterone by the enzyme 5α-reductase.

FSH and Leydig cells (Option C): Leydig cells are stimulated by LH, not FSH. FSH primarily acts on Sertoli cells to aid spermatogenesis.

question_text: Almost all eukaryotic mRNA molecules, at 3'-hydroxyl terminus have an attached, non genetically encoded polymer of adenylate residues (20 to 250 nucleotides in length), which is known as poly(A) tail. Eukaryotic mRNAs have unique chemical characteristics.

The cap is involved in the recognition of mRNA by the translation machinery, and also helps stabilize the mRNA by preventing the nucleolytic attack by 5′-exoribonucleases. The protein-synthesizing machinery begins translating the mRNA into proteins beginning downstream of the 5′ or capped terminus. 

At the other end of almost all eukaryotic mRNA molecules, the 3′-hydroxyl terminus has an attached, non genetically encoded polymer of adenylate residues 20 to 250 nucleotides in length. The poly(A) “tail” at the 3′-end of mRNAs maintains the intracellular stability of the specific mRNA by preventing the attack of 3′-exoribonucleases and also facilitates translation. A few mRNAs, including those for some histones, do not contain poly (A) tail.

The chemical nature of RNA differs from that of DNA

RNA is a polymer of purine and pyrimidine ribonucleotides linked together by 3′,5′-phosphodiester bonds analogous to those in DNA. Although sharing many features with DNA, RNA possesses several specific differences:

In RNA, the sugar moiety to which the phosphates and purine and pyrimidine bases are attached is ribose rather than the 2′-deoxyribose of DNA.

The pyrimidine components of RNA can differ from those of DNA. Although RNA contains the ribonucleotides of adenine, guanine, and cytosine, it does not possess thymine except in the rare case. Instead of thymine, RNA contains the ribonucleotide of uracil.

RNA typically exists as a single strand, whereas DNA exists as a double-stranded helical molecule.

Since the RNA molecule is a single strand complementary to only one of the two strands of a gene, its guanine content does not necessarily equal its cytosine content, nor does its adenine content necessarily equal its uracil content.

RNA can be hydrolyzed by alkali to 2′, 3′ cyclic di esters of the mononucleotides, compounds that cannot be formed from alkali-treated DNA because of the absence of a 2′-hydroxyl group. The alkali lability of RNA is useful both diagnostically and analytically.

question_text: Which of the following is a purine base?

question_text: A boy presents with stretchable skin and flexible fingers with which he can reach his forearm. What is the most probable diagnosis?

EDS is a group of inherited connective tissue disorders primarily caused by defects in the synthesis or structure of collagen (most commonly type V collagen) or other connective tissue proteins. This leads to the hallmark features of skin hyperelasticity, joint hypermobility, and tissue fragility.

Explanation of other options:

Marfan syndrome (Option D): Marfan syndrome is characterized by tall stature, arachnodactyly(long, slender fingers), lens dislocation, and aortic root dilation. While joint laxity can occur, the skin is not typically described as hyperextensible, and the overall phenotype is distinct from EDS.

Key Takeaways:

  • Ehlers-Danlos syndrome is classically associated with the triad of hyperelastic skin, joint hypermobility, and tissue fragility.
  • The "thumb sign" (ability to appose the thumb to the flexor aspect of the forearm) is a test for joint hypermobility.

question_text: Death caused by Carbon monoxide and cyanide is because they affect:
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Cyanide (CN-) and Carbon Monoxide (CO) are classic examples of histotoxic hypoxia inducers, where the cells are unable to utilize oxygen despite adequate delivery.
  • Mechanism of Toxicity: Both toxins are potent inhibitors of the mitochondrial electron transport chain (ETC), specifically targeting the cytochrome proteins
  • Specific Site of Action:
  • Carbon monoxide binds to the heme iron of cytochrome c oxidase in its reduced (ferrous Fe2+) state.
  • Cyanide binds irreversibly with high affinity to the ferric iron (Fe3+) heme group within the cytochrome a3 component of Cytochrome c Oxidase (Complex IV).
  • Consequence: This binding blocks the final step of electron transfer to molecular oxygen (O2). As a result, the entire ETC grinds to a halt. Oxygen cannot be reduced to water, proton pumping ceases, the proton gradient across the inner mitochondrial membrane collapses, and ATP synthesis via oxidative phosphorylation stops. This rapid failure of cellular energy production is fatal, particularly for organs with high energy demands like the brain and heart.

Explanation of other options:

Myoglobin (Option A): Myoglobin is an oxygen-binding protein in muscle. While carbon monoxide has a very high affinity for myoglobin (and hemoglobin), binding to it and impairing oxygen storage and delivery, this is not the primary cause of rapid death. Cyanide does not significantly bind to myoglobin.

NADH Dehydrogenase (Option C): This refers to Complex I of the ETC. While there are specific inhibitors for Complex I (e.g., rotenone, amobarbital), neither cyanide nor carbon monoxide acts at this site.

ATPase (Option D): This refers to ATP Synthase (Complex V), the enzyme that synthesizes ATP using the proton gradient. Cyanide and CO do not directly inhibit ATP synthase.

Key Takeaways:

  • Cyanide and CO cause death by inhibiting cytochrome oxidase (Complex IV), halting cellular respiration.
  • Inhibitors of Electron transport chain

question_text: Progress through the mammalian cell cycle is continuously monitored via multiple cell-cycle checkpoints. Which of the following cyclin dependent kinases (CDK) regulates transition of cell cycle from G2 to M phase?

Option A: CDK1 involve in transition from G2 to M

Option B: CDK2 involves the initiation of DNA synthesis in the early S phase.

Option C & Option D: CDK4 & CDK6 are involved in progression past the restriction point in G1/S boundary.

All eukaryotic cells have gene products that govern the transition from one phase of the cell cycle to another. The cyclins are a family of proteins whose concentration increases and decreases at specific times, that is, "cycle" during the cell cycle - thus their name. The cyclins thus activate, at the appropriate time, different cyclin-dependent protein kinases (CDKs) that phosphorylate substrates essential for progression through the cell cycle.

For example, cyclin D levels rise in late G1 phase and allow progression beyond the start (yeast) or restriction point (mammals), the point beyond which cells irrevocably proceed into the S or DNA synthesis phase.

The D cyclins activate CDK4 and CDK6. These two kinases are also synthesized during G1 in cells undergoing active division. The D cyclins and CDK4 and CDK6 are nuclear proteins that assemble as a complex in late G1 phase. The cyclin-CDK complex is now an active serine - threonine protein kinase. One substrate for this kinase is the retinoblastoma (Rb) protein. Rb is a cell-cycle regulator because it binds to and inactivates a transcription factor (E2F) necessary for the transcription of certain genes (histone genes, DNA replication proteins, etc) needed for progression from G1 to S phase. The phosphorylation of Rb by CDK4 or CDK6 results in the release of E2F from Rb-mediated transcription repression - thus, gene transcription activation ensues and cell-cycle progression takes place.

Cyclin E and CDK2 form a complex in late G1. Cyclin E is rapidly degraded, and the released CDK2 then forms a complex with cyclin A. This sequence is necessary for the initiation of DNA synthesis in S phase. A complex between cyclin B and CDK1 is rate-limiting for the G2/M transition in eukaryotic cells.

Many of the cancer-causing viruses (oncoviruses) and cancer-inducing genes (oncogenes) are capable of alleviating or disrupting the restriction that normally controls the entry of mammalian cells from G1 into the S phase. From the foregoing, one might have surmised that excessive production of a cyclin, loss of a specific CDK inhibitor, or production or activation of a cyclin/CDK at an inappropriate time might result in abnormal or unrestrained cell division. Similarly, the oncoproteins (or transforming proteins) produced by several DNA viruses target the Rb transcription repressor for inactivation, inducing cell division inappropriately, while inactivation of Rb, itself a tumor suppressor gene, leads to uncontrolled cell growth and tumor formation.

  • Urea cycle occurs only in liver. First two step in mitochondria and next three steps in cytoplasm.
  • The summary reaction of the urea cycle is: NH44⁺+ HCO3⁻ + aspartate + 3 ATP → urea + fumarate + 2 ADP + AMP + 4 Pi.
  • Urea cycle also known as the ornithine cycle.
  • Ammonia is a byproduct of amino acid catabolism.
  • High levels of ammonia are toxic to cells, especially in the brain, where it can disrupt neurotransmission and lead to a condition called hepatic encephalopathy.
  • Glycogen (carbohydrate sources) can convert into glucose by glycogenolysis. A non-carbohydrate sources like lactate, glycerol, glucogenic amino acids & propionate can convert into glucose by gluconeogenesis. An ammonia cannot convert into glucose. (Option A)
  • Ammonia is toxic at higher concentration, so cannot be stored in tissues. (Option B)
  • It synthesizes amino acid arginine from carbon dioxide and ammonia. Not from urea and carbon dioxide. (Option C)

question_text:
A young female came to OPD with symptoms of vomiting, lethargy , irritability and severe mental retardation. On investigation her blood ammonia level is increased along with changes of alkalosis. Patient is responding very well to administration of N acetylglutamate.
Which of the following enzymes is deficient in this patient?
explanation:
Clinical symptoms common to all urea cycle disorders include vomiting, intermittent ataxia, irritability, lethargy, and severe mental retardation.

The most dramatic clinical presentation occurs in full-term infants who initially appear normal, then exhibit progressive lethargy, hypothermia, and apnea due to high plasma ammonia levels.

The clinical features and treatment of all five disorders are similar. Significant improvement and minimization of brain damage can accompany a low-protein diet ingested as frequent small meals to avoid sudden increases in blood ammonia levels. The goal of dietary therapy is to provide sufficient protein, arginine, and energy to promote growth and development while simultaneously minimizing the metabolic perturbations.

N-Acetylglutamate Synthase (NAGS) -

Catalyzes the formation of N-acetylglutamate (essential for carbamoyl phosphate synthase I activity) from acetyl-CoA and glutamate.

L-Glutamate + Acetyl-CoA → N-acetyl-L-glutamate + CoASH

While the clinical and biochemical features of NAGS deficiency are indistinguishable from those arising from a defect in carbamoyl phosphate synthase I, a deficiency in NAGS may respond to administration of N-acetylglutamate.

Reference: Harper's 32nd edition, page 295

question_text: Which of the following is true about pyrimidine biosynthesis?
option_a: Energetically costlier than de novo purine biosynthesis
option_b: CPS II is a mitochondrial enzyme
option_c: PRPP serves as a scaffold for assembly of the pyrimidine ring
option_d: Multifunctional proteins catalyze early reaction of pyrimidine biosynthesis
explanation:
Option A: Compared to biosynthesis of pyrimidines, purine nucleoside biosynthesis is energetically more costly

Option B: The catalyst for the initial reaction is cytosolic carbamoyl phosphate synthetase II.

A different enzyme carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I, used in urea synthesis (urea cycle) is present in mitochondria.

Such compartmentation thus provides an independent pool of carbamoyl phosphate for each process.

Option C: PRPP serves as a scaffold for assembly of the purine ring in purine biosynthesis. Whereas PRPP participates in pyrimidine biosynthesis only subsequent to assembly of the pyrimidine ring.

Option D: Multifunctional proteins catalyze the early reactions of pyrimidine biosynthesis.

Five of the first six enzyme activities of pyrimidine biosynthesis reside on multifunctional polypeptides. The close proximity of multiple active sites on a multifunctional polypeptide facilitates efficient channeling of the intermediates of pyrimidine biosynthesis.

Reference: Harper's illustrated biochemistry 32nd edition CH 33 PN 332

question_text: Identify the amino acid derivative
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Amino acid derivatives are molecules that are structurally related to amino acids but have been chemically modified.
  • Amino acid derivatives are involved in various biological functions, including neurotransmission, hormone activity, metabolism, and as intermediates in biosynthetic pathways.

Various examples of amino acid derivatives:

  • Serotonin: Synthesized from tryptophan and regulates mood, sleep, and appetite.
  • Epinephrine and Norepinephrine: Derived from tyrosine, act as hormones and neurotransmitters regulating stress response.
  • Thyroxine (T4) and Triiodothyronine (T3): Hormones derived from tyrosine and iodine, produced by the thyroid gland, and regulate metabolism.
  • Melatonin: Derived from tryptophan, this hormone is involved in regulating the sleep-wake cycle.
  • Ornithine and Citrulline: Derived from arginine, they are intermediates in the urea cycle.
  • Creatine: Derived from glycine and arginine, it plays a role in energy storage, particularly in muscle tissues.
  • Beta-Alanine: A component of carnosine, involved in muscle endurance.
  • Hydroxyproline: Derived from proline, essential for the stability of collagen.
  • Gamma-Carboxyglutamate: A derivative of glutamate important in calcium-binding proteins involved in blood clotting.
  • Carnosine: A dipeptide (beta-alanine and histidine) with antioxidant and anti-aging properties.
  • L-Carnitine: Derived from lysine and methionine, important for the transport of fatty acids into mitochondria for energy production.
  • N-Acetylcysteine: A modified form of cysteine that acts as a precursor to glutathione and is used to treat acetaminophen overdose and chronic respiratory conditions.

Key take away

  • Serotonin & Melatonin: Synthesized from tryptophan
  • Dopamine, Epinephrine and Norepinephrine, Thyroid hormones: Derived from tyrosine
  • Ornithine and Citrulline: Derived from arginine
  • GABA: derived from glutamic acid, inhibitory neurotransmitters

question_text: Nitric oxide, a key signalling molecule involved in vasodilation, is endogenously synthesized from which amino acid precursor?
explanation:
Explanation:

The correct precursor is L-arginine. Nitric oxide (NO) is synthesized in a reaction catalyzed by the enzyme nitric oxide synthase (NOS), which converts L-arginine into NO and L-citrulline, utilizing molecular oxygen and NADPH.

The Nitric Oxide function by diffusing into adjacent smooth muscle cells and activates guanylate cyclase which leads to an increase in cyclic GMP levels, which activates protein kinase in smooth muscle and this causes the dephosphorylation of myosin light chains, resulting in relaxation of smooth

Explanation of other options:

L-citrulline (Option B): L-citrulline is a byproduct of the NO synthesis reaction, not the precursor. It can be recycled back to arginine in the urea cycle.

Glycine (Option C): Glycine is not involved in NO synthesis, it is a neurotransmitter and a precursor for heme and purine synthesis.

Lysine (Option D): Lysine is not a precursor for NO, it is an essential amino acid involved in protein synthesis and other metabolic pathways.

question_text: Which cofactor is essential for the activity of carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I, the first enzyme of the urea cycle?
explanation:
Explanation:

Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I, the rate-limiting enzyme of the urea cycle, is active only in the presence of N-acetylglutamate, an allosteric activator that enhances the affinity of the synthetase for ATP.

  • Synthesis of 1 mol of carbamoyl phosphate requires 2 mol of ATP.
  • One ATP serves as the phosphoryl donor for formation of the mixed acid anhydride bond of carbamoyl phosphate.
  • The second ATP provides the driving force for synthesis of the amide bond of carbamoyl phosphate.

Key take away

  • NADH, FADH2 are coenzyme for dehydrogenase group of enzymes
  • Biotin is coenzyme for carboxylase enzymes
  • ATP is coenzyme for synthetase enzymes

question_text: Substrate linking Krebs's cycle with urea cycle is:
explanation:
Option A: Aspartate is an amino acid, involved in the urea cycle.

Argininosuccinate synthetase links aspartate and citrulline via the amino group of aspartate and provides the second nitrogen of urea.

Option B: Cleavage of argininosuccinate is catalyzed by argininosuccinate lyase in the urea cycle. The reaction proceeds with retention of all three nitrogens in arginine and release of the aspartate skeleton as fumarate. Subsequent addition of water to fumarate forms l-malate, whose subsequent NAD+-dependent oxidation forms oxaloacetate. These two reactions are analogous to reactions of the citric acid cycle, but are catalyzed by cytosolic fumarase and malate dehydrogenase. Transamination of oxaloacetate by glutamate aminotransferase then reforms aspartate. The carbon skeleton of aspartate-fumarate thus acts as a carrier of the nitrogen of glutamate into a precursor of urea.

Option C: Alanine is an amino acid, not involved in urea cycle or kreb’s cycle.

Option D: Cleavage of argininosuccinate is catalyzed by argininosuccinate lyase in the urea cycle. The reaction proceeds with retention of all three nitrogens in arginine. So arginine is involved in only the urea cycle.
